lesson.title: The Repeating Cycle: Higher Derivatives of Sine and Cosine
lesson.summary: The derivatives of sine and cosine never wander off into new territory: they cycle through the same four functions forever, so you can find any derivative, no matter how high the order, with simple remainder arithmetic.
lesson.body:
Most functions get more complicated the more times you differentiate them. Take a polynomial like x^5: each derivative knocks the degree down by one, and after six derivatives you are left with zero. Sine and cosine behave completely differently, and once you see why, higher order derivatives of these functions become almost trivial to compute, which is a nice payoff after the work you put into the nth derivative idea in general and into finding the derivative of sine in particular.

Start with sine and just keep differentiating. The derivative of sin x is cos x. The derivative of cos x is negative sin x. The derivative of negative sin x is negative cos x. The derivative of negative cos x is sin x again, right back where you started. Written as a chain:

sin x, then cos x, then -sin x, then -cos x, then sin x, then cos x, and so on, repeating every four derivatives.

Cosine does the same dance, just starting one step later in the cycle: cos x, then -sin x, then -cos x, then sin x, then cos x again. Because both families repeat with period four, the entire problem of finding a high order derivative collapses into one question: what is the remainder when you divide the order n by 4?

There is also a compact formula that captures this cycling automatically, using the fact that adding pi over 2 to the input of sine or cosine shifts it exactly one step along the cycle: the nth derivative of sin x equals sin(x + n pi/2), and the nth derivative of cos x equals cos(x + n pi/2). You can check this against the list above: plugging in n = 1 gives sin(x + pi/2), which is indeed cos x, and n = 2 gives sin(x + pi), which is indeed -sin x. Either the remainder table or this shifted formula will get you the same answer, so use whichever is easier to remember.

Here are two worked examples that show the shortcut in action. First, find the 100th derivative of sin x. Divide 100 by 4: the remainder is 0, which corresponds to the starting point of the cycle, so the 100th derivative of sin x is just sin x again. Second, find the 37th derivative of cos x. Divide 37 by 4: 4 goes in 9 times with a remainder of 1, and remainder 1 in the cosine cycle (cos x, -sin x, -cos x, sin x) lands on the second entry, so the 37th derivative of cos x is -sin x. You can double check this with the shifted formula: cos(x + 37 pi/2). Since 37 pi/2 equals 18 pi plus pi/2, and cosine has period 2 pi so the 18 pi contributes nothing, this reduces to cos(x + pi/2), which is -sin x, matching the remainder method exactly.

This pattern is worth internalizing early, because trig functions show up constantly in later work that depends on knowing higher derivatives quickly and correctly, and being able to jump straight to the 100th derivative without writing out 100 lines of differentiation is exactly the kind of structural shortcut calculus rewards you for noticing.
